title: Journey to the End of the Earth
summary: Tishani Doshi describes her voyage to Antarctica with the Students on Ice programme. The visit teaches her about the earth's geological past and present, and convinces her that Antarctica is the best place to understand climate change and the future of the planet.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Tishani Doshi (born 1975) is an Indian poet, writer and dancer based in Chennai. This travel essay records her journey to the coldest, driest and windiest continent.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: The writer travels from Madras to Antarctica aboard a Russian research vessel with a group of high-school students. Standing in the vast white landscape, she reflects on how India and Antarctica were once part of one landmass, how human activity is warming the planet, and why young people should see this place for themselves.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
• The journey: Starting from 13.09 degrees north of the Equator, she crosses nine time zones, six checkpoints, three bodies of water and at least as many ecospheres, travelling for over a hundred hours by car, aeroplane and ship. Her first feeling on arrival is relief, followed by wonder at the immensity and isolation.
  • Part of history: About six hundred and fifty million years ago a giant southern supercontinent, Gondwana, existed, centred roughly on present-day Antarctica. The climate was warmer and there was a great variety of plants and animals. Around the time dinosaurs died out and mammals rose, it broke up into countries as we know them. Antarctica keeps this record in its ice.
  • Human impact: Humans have existed for only a few seconds on the geological clock, yet they have dominated nature with cities and megacities, burnt fossil fuels and created a blanket of carbon dioxide that is raising the average global temperature.
  • Why Antarctica matters: It has never sustained a human population, so it is relatively pristine. It holds half-million-year-old carbon records in its layers of ice. If its ice sheets melt, the consequences for the world will be drastic.
  • Students on Ice: The programme, led by Canadian Geoff Green, takes students to the ends of the world so that the future generation of policy-makers develops understanding and respect for the planet at an age when they can absorb, learn and act.
  • Phytoplankton: These microscopic sea grasses use the sun's energy to absorb carbon and make organic compounds, supporting the entire Southern Ocean food chain. Depletion of the ozone layer would affect them and, through them, all marine life and the global carbon cycle. The lesson: take care of small things and the big things will fall into place.
  • Walk on the ocean: Near the Antarctic Circle the ship gets wedged in thick ice. Everyone climbs down and walks on a metre of ice with deep sea water beneath, while seals sunbathe on the floes nearby. The experience shows her how everything is connected.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Climate change and global warming: Antarctica is the place where the threat can be seen and measured.
  • Interconnectedness of life: a change in tiny organisms can affect the whole planet.
  • The earth's past, present and future: the continent is a storehouse of geological history.
  • Responsibility of youth: education by direct experience builds lasting concern.

notes.heading: Why Antarctica is the place to study the earth
notes.html:

notes.heading: Title and message
notes.html: The title describes both a physical journey to the southern edge of the world and a mental journey to the 'end' in time: back to the earth's beginnings and forward to its possible fate. The message is that the planet's health depends on our choices, and that awareness must begin early.

questions.q: What were the writer's feelings on reaching Antarctica?
questions.answerHtml: Her first emotion was relief after more than a hundred hours of travel. It soon gave way to deep wonder at the continent's vastness, its isolation and, above all, the fact that India and Antarctica were once part of the same landmass.

questions.q: Why is Antarctica crucial to the debate on climate change?
questions.answerHtml: It is the only place that has never sustained a human population, so it remains relatively unspoilt. Its ice cores hold half-million-year-old carbon records, and it stores most of the earth's ice, so it shows us the past and warns us about the future.

questions.q: How was the walk on the ocean a revelation?
questions.answerHtml: Walking on a metre-thick sheet of ice with a deep, living ocean beneath it, and seals resting nearby, the writer realised that everything on the planet is linked. A small change in one part of this delicate system can affect all the rest.

questions.q: 'The world's geological history is trapped in Antarctica.' How is the study of this region useful to us?
questions.answerHtml:
Antarctica is a window on the earth's past. It was once the heart of Gondwana, a warm supercontinent with rich plant and animal life. Its rocks and ice preserve evidence of how continents drifted apart and how climates changed over millions of years.

The layers of ice contain carbon records going back half a million years. By studying them, scientists can compare today's levels of greenhouse gases with those of the past and judge the speed of change. Because the continent has never had a human population and has a simple ecosystem, the effects of even small changes are clearly visible there.

The study is useful for the future as well. Antarctica holds about ninety per cent of the world's ice. If warming melts it, sea levels will rise everywhere. Watching its glaciers retreat and ice shelves collapse makes the danger real. Understanding Antarctica therefore helps us understand where we came from and where we may be heading.

questions.q: Why does the author think that programmes like Students on Ice are valuable? What does the essay say about small things in nature?
questions.answerHtml:
The author feels that reading about polar ice caps melting, while living comfortably far away, makes little impression. Seeing glaciers retreat and ice shelves collapse with one's own eyes changes a person. Students are at an age when they are ready to absorb, learn and act, and they are the policy-makers of tomorrow. The programme gives them a life-changing experience so that they grow up with understanding and respect for the planet.

The essay also teaches the importance of small things through the example of phytoplankton. These microscopic plants use sunlight to take in carbon and produce food, and they nourish the entire marine life of the Southern Ocean. If ozone depletion reduces their activity, the whole food chain and the global carbon cycle will be disturbed.

The writer concludes that if we take care of the small things, the big things will fall into place. Protecting the environment begins with respecting its tiniest parts.
